# Post-Voxelization Modifiers
## Overview
Post-Voxelization Modifiers are algorithms applied to a discrete voxel grid after the initial geometric conversion to correct artifacts, optimize storage, or adapt the data for specific rendering pipelines [G]. This family modifies existing voxel attributes (density, material, opacity) without re-evaluating the source geometry [G]. It encompasses interactive editing, LOD downsampling, porosity injection, surface thickening, and multi-volume compositing [G].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family apply a transformation rule to an existing voxel grid after initial geometric conversion, without re-evaluating the source geometry [G]. The execution model typically involves reading an input grid, applying a local or global transformation rule (such as neighborhood analysis or statistical aggregation), and writing a modified grid or rendering mask [G].

## Subtopics

### [Voxel Editing Tools](17731-voxel-editing-tools.md)
Voxel Editing Tools provide interactive, post-voxelization modification of volumetric data, allowing users to surgically alter individual or grouped voxels for tasks such as surgical planning, artifact correction, or data abstraction. Unlike the parent family which often applies algorithmic, non-interactive transformations, this method relies on direct user input via a stylus or pointer to define local regions of influence. It distinguishes itself from siblings like [Avatar Head Data Variant Application](22734-avatar-head-data-variant-application.md) by focusing on arbitrary spatial manipulation (removal, transparency, recoloring) rather than variant-specific attribute mapping. Choose this method when direct user-driven local edits are required [G]. See [Voxel Editing Tools](17731-voxel-editing-tools.md).

### [Avatar Head Data Variant Application](22734-avatar-head-data-variant-application.md)
This method modifies a base head voxel data array to apply specific hair variants (short, buzz, or long) by rewriting specific voxel value markers. It solves the problem of dynamically changing character appearance without re-voxelizing the underlying geometry, allowing for iterative refinement or user-driven adjustments post-generation. It is distinct from general [Voxel Editing Tools](17731-voxel-editing-tools.md) by focusing exclusively on semantic hair type substitution within the head region using predefined integer markers. Choose this method when dynamically changing character appearance without re-voxelizing geometry is required [G]. See [Avatar Head Data Variant Application](22734-avatar-head-data-variant-application.md).

### Voxel Downsampling with Material Propagation
A hierarchical compression technique used in large-scale planetary voxel systems to reduce memory footprint while preserving visual fidelity across distance levels [S1, unofficial]. It operates on a hierarchy of voxel grids (bricks) where each coarse voxel represents a 2x2x2 block of finer voxels [S1, unofficial]. A coarse voxel is classified as solid if at least 4 of its 8 children are solid [S1, unofficial]. The material of the coarse voxel is determined by the most common material among its solid children [S1, unofficial]. Edits to the fine grid propagate immediately up all LOD levels, ensuring that features like craters remain visible from orbit without requiring separate mesh fallbacks [S1, unofficial]. Chosen for open-world or planetary rendering where memory budget is strict (e.g., ~2 GB on a 4090) and distance-based detail is required [S1, unofficial]. See [Sparse and Hierarchical Structures](4391-sparse-and-hierarchical-structures.md) for the underlying data structure [G].

### Porosity via Spatial Pseudo-Random Hash Drop-out
A technique to introduce controlled void space into voxelized meshes, simulating porous materials or reducing voxel count for aesthetic or performant reasons [S2, unofficial]. Voxels are dropped (set to empty) based on a spatial pseudo-random hash function [S2, unofficial]. The decision is deterministic for a given coordinate, ensuring consistency across updates [S2, unofficial]. Controlled by a `porosity` float parameter, passed via CLI (`--porosity <FLOAT>`) or API (`MeshProcessor::voxelize`) [S2, unofficial]. Chosen when simulating materials like foam or rock, or when reducing voxel density for performance without altering the mesh geometry [S2, unofficial]. See [VoxelGrid from Mesh (Fill Method)](1013-voxelgrid-from-mesh-fill-method.md) for the base generation method [G].

### Opacify Modifier
A correction step for rendering thin or zero-thickness geometry (such as meshes) that would otherwise appear dashed, aliased, or partially transparent during ray marching or cone marching [S3, unofficial]. Meshes are hollow; voxelization gives partly covered voxels; the modifier scales coverage up so grazed surfaces read as solid, effectively thickening the voxel representation of the surface [S3, unofficial]. The `Amount` parameter (default 2.0f) controls the thickening [S3, unofficial]. Increasing this value prevents surface leakage but may cause inflation; decreasing it reduces inflation but may reveal transparency [S3, unofficial]. It is not a substitute for sufficient voxel resolution [S3, unofficial]. Chosen when rendering wireframes, thin shells, or low-poly meshes where standard voxelization fails to produce a solid appearance [S3, unofficial]. See [Voxel Volume Rendering](6488-voxel-volume-rendering.md) for the rendering context [G].

### Decluttering
A technique to highlight structures of interest by combining the original volume with a second volume containing complementary information (e.g., distance to a structure) to modulate the rendering [S4]. Provide two input volumes: the original volume and a second volume containing complementary data [S4]. In the Volume shader for the second volume, multiply the color-mapped sample from the second volume with the accumulated sample from the first volume: `vec4 sample = SampleVolumeWithTF (volIndex, pos); fullSample * = sample;` [S4]. Do not use raw samples from the second volume to modulate color or opacity; use the color-mapped sample (after transfer function application) to allow interactive adjustment of decluttering via the transfer function [S4].

### Gaussian Smearing for Interface Blurring
A preprocessing step to simulate the blurring of interfaces between different materials (e.g., rock and fluid) caused by finite voxel resolution in X-ray imaging [S5]. Identify the interface between the rock matrix and fluid phases in the simulation volume [S5]. Apply a Gaussian filter to the interface region to smear the boundary, creating voxels that contain mixed material properties [S5].

## Background
Post-voxelization processing evolved as voxelization shifted from simple binary occupancy grids to complex, attribute-rich representations for real-time rendering and global illumination [G]. Hierarchical downsampling techniques emerged for large-scale planetary systems to manage memory budgets across distance levels [S1, unofficial]. The Opacify modifier was introduced in real-time voxel GI systems like StrideVoxelGI to handle visual artifacts from rasterizing thin geometry into voxels [S3, unofficial]. Porosity injection via spatial hashing was added to open-source voxelizers to control material void space [S2, unofficial]. Decluttering and Gaussian smearing techniques were developed for medical and scientific volume rendering to enhance interpretability of complex structures and simulate partial volume effects [S4, S5].
